blocks.text: 1. F1 Score

blocks.alt: Precision and recall combine through a harmonic mean into F1 score

blocks.text: Precision and Recall, the previous two topics, each capture one genuine half of the picture of classifier quality, and the closing section of the Recall topic established that pulling one of these two metrics up, through adjusting the decision threshold, typically pulls the other one down as a direct, largely unavoidable consequence. F1 Score exists specifically to resolve the awkwardness of having to report and weigh two separate, competing numbers, combining precision and recall together into a single, balanced metric.

This makes F1 Score the natural closing piece to the precision-recall story covered across the last two topics, and it has become one of the most widely reported classification metrics in practice precisely because it gives a fair, single-number summary that genuinely accounts for both the trustworthiness of positive predictions and the thoroughness of catching genuine positive cases, rather than letting either dimension hide behind the other.
2. The Harmonic Mean, Not a Simple Average

blocks.alt: A simple average is compared against the harmonic mean

blocks.text: A first, seemingly natural instinct for combining precision and recall into one number might be to take their simple average, adding the two values together and dividing by 2. F1 Score deliberately uses a different kind of average instead, called the harmonic mean, computed as 2 times the product of precision and recall, divided by the sum of precision and recall.

This specific choice of averaging method is not arbitrary; the harmonic mean has a genuinely important mathematical property that a simple average lacks, one that makes it far better suited to this specific combination task, covered directly in the next section with a concrete, illustrative example.
3. Why the Harmonic Mean Specifically

Consider a deliberately extreme, lopsided model with a precision of 1.0, every single positive prediction it makes is correct, but a recall of only 0.01, it catches a mere 1 percent of all the genuine positive cases that actually exist. A simple average of these two numbers works out to 0.505, a result that looks deceptively reasonable, roughly in the middle of the 0 to 1 scale, hiding just how badly lopsided and genuinely limited this particular model actually is.

The harmonic mean, F1 Score's actual formula, produces a dramatically different result for this exact same model: approximately 0.02, a number that correctly, honestly reflects just how close to useless this model actually is in practice, despite its flawless precision. This is precisely the harmonic mean's key mathematical property: it is dominated by whichever of the two input values is smaller, punishing a large imbalance between precision and recall far more severely than a simple average ever would, exactly the behavior needed to catch and expose situations like this one.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: The harmonic mean's sensitivity to the smaller of the two input values means F1 Score can only be genuinely high when both precision and recall are reasonably high simultaneously. A model cannot compensate for a terrible recall with an excellent precision, or vice versa, the way a simple average would allow.

blocks.text: 4. A Genuinely Balanced Score

blocks.alt: F1 score balances precision and recall together

blocks.text: The direct, practical consequence of the harmonic mean's mathematical property, covered in the previous section, is that F1 Score is only ever high when both precision and recall are reasonably high at the same time. If either precision or recall drops to a very low value, F1 Score drops sharply as a direct result, regardless of how excellent the other metric happens to be.

When both precision and recall sit at reasonably balanced, comparable levels, F1 Score stays correspondingly reasonably high, honestly reflecting genuine, well-rounded classifier performance across both dimensions simultaneously, rather than performance that excels in one specific direction while badly neglecting the other. This balancing property is precisely what makes F1 Score such a trustworthy single-number summary of overall classifier quality whenever both precision and recall genuinely matter.
5. When F1 Score Is the Right Metric to Report

blocks.alt: Needing both precision and recall balanced points toward using F1 score

blocks.text: F1 Score is the natural choice whenever there is no strong, specific reason to weigh false positives differently from false negatives for the problem at hand, situations where a single number fairly balancing both error types genuinely captures what matters, rather than needing the sharper, more specific focus precision or recall alone would provide for a problem where one error type is clearly, substantially worse than the other.

It is also the practical choice whenever reporting a single headline number is more useful than juggling two separate metrics, exactly the situation common in model comparison tables and competition leaderboards. And it is a genuinely strong choice specifically on imbalanced datasets where plain accuracy, covered in the first topic of this module, cannot be trusted, since F1 Score, unlike accuracy, is built directly from precision and recall rather than from raw overall correctness, which makes it structurally resistant to the exact majority-class inflation problem that plagued accuracy.
6. F-beta: When Precision and Recall Should Not Be Weighed Equally

blocks.alt: F-beta can weigh precision more or weigh recall more

blocks.text: F1 Score, by design, always weighs precision and recall exactly equally, treating both dimensions as equally important regardless of the specific problem at hand. But recall from the Precision and Recall topics that some problems genuinely have one of these two error types mattering substantially more than the other, disease screening favoring recall, spam filtering favoring precision, exactly the asymmetric-cost situations covered in depth in those two earlier topics.

The F-beta score generalizes F1 Score to handle exactly this situation, introducing a tunable parameter, beta, that controls the relative weight given to recall versus precision. F2 Score, using a beta value of 2, is a common practical choice that weighs recall as twice as important as precision, well suited to disease-screening-style problems where missing a genuine positive is especially costly. F0.5 Score, using a beta value of 0.5, weighs precision as twice as important as recall instead, well suited to spam-filtering-style problems where a false alarm is especially costly.

blocks.text: 7. F1 Score Is Not a Complete Picture Either

blocks.alt: F1 score hides which of precision or recall is actually lower

blocks.text: Despite its genuine strengths, F1 Score is not a flawless, complete summary of classifier quality on its own, and it is worth understanding its own specific limitation directly before moving further into this module. F1 Score is built entirely from precision and recall, which means, exactly like both of those individual metrics, it still does not directly account for True Negatives at all, the fourth confusion matrix category first previewed back in the Accuracy topic.

This means two models with identical precision and identical recall, but very different behavior on the negative class, genuinely different numbers of True Negatives relative to the dataset, receive the exact same F1 Score, despite potentially meaningful differences in how well they handle the negative class overall. This specific gap, F1 Score's continued blindness to True Negative behavior, is one of the motivations behind Cohen Kappa, covered later in this module, which incorporates all four confusion matrix categories together in a different, more complete way.
8. F1 Score Beyond Binary Classification

F1 Score extends to multiclass classification building directly on the same per-class approach already covered for multiclass Precision and Recall in their own topics: compute F1 separately for each class, treating that specific class as positive and every other class combined as negative, then combine these per-class F1 values into one overall number.

Three standard combination approaches exist. Macro-averaging takes the simple, unweighted average across every class's F1 score, treating every class as equally important regardless of size. Weighted-averaging weights each class's F1 by how many examples that class actually contains, giving larger classes more influence. Micro-averaging takes a different approach entirely, first pooling every True Positive, False Positive, and False Negative together across all classes into single combined totals, then computing one single F1 Score from those pooled totals, a method that effectively weighs every individual prediction equally rather than every class equally.
9. A Quick Reference Across the Four Metrics Covered So Far

blocks.alt: Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score are the four metrics covered so far

blocks.text: With Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and now F1 Score all covered, it is worth summarizing the relationship between them directly before moving to the remaining topics in this module. Accuracy measures overall correctness across every prediction, but remains vulnerable to being badly inflated by class imbalance. Precision measures specifically how trustworthy the model's positive predictions are, ignoring the negative class entirely.

Recall measures specifically how thoroughly the model catches genuine positive cases, ignoring how it handles the negative class. F1 Score combines precision and recall together into a single, harmonically balanced number, resolving the awkwardness of reporting two separate, competing metrics, though it too still ignores True Negatives entirely, a gap Cohen Kappa, covered later in this module, is built specifically to address.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example

The example below computes F1 Score alongside precision and recall for the same disease-screening classifier used in the Recall topic's worked example, and compares it against the F2 Score, which weighs recall more heavily.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, fbeta_score, precision_score, recall_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X_healthy = rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=2, size=(180, 2))
X_sick = rng.normal(loc=[4, 4], scale=2, size=(20, 2))
X = np.vstack([X_healthy, X_sick])
y = np.array([0] * 180 + [1] * 20)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=y)

model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
predictions = model.predict(X_test)

precision = precision_score(y_test, predictions, zero_division=0)
recall = recall_score(y_test, predictions)
f1 = f1_score(y_test, predictions)
f2 = fbeta_score(y_test, predictions, beta=2)  # weighs recall twice as heavily as precision

print(f"Precision: {precision:.3f}")
print(f"Recall:    {recall:.3f}")
print(f"F1 Score:  {f1:.3f} (equal weight on both)")
print(f"F2 Score:  {f2:.3f} (favors recall, appropriate for disease screening)")

# Demonstrate why harmonic mean matters: compare against a naive simple average
simple_average = (precision + recall) / 2
print(f"\nSimple average of precision and recall: {simple_average:.3f}")
print(f"F1 Score (harmonic mean): {f1:.3f}")
print("Notice the harmonic mean is pulled toward whichever of the two is smaller")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: F2 Score, weighing recall more heavily, is generally the more appropriate metric for this disease-screening context, since catching genuinely sick patients matters more here than avoiding the occasional false alarm, exactly the F-beta weighting logic covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: F1 Score combines precision and recall into a single, balanced number using the harmonic mean, not a simple average.
The harmonic mean punishes a large imbalance between precision and recall far more severely than a simple average would.
F1 Score is only high when both precision and recall are reasonably high simultaneously, rewarding genuine, well-rounded performance.
It suits problems with no strong asymmetric cost between error types, single-number reporting, and imbalanced data where accuracy fails.
F-beta generalizes F1 Score with a tunable weight: F2 favors recall, F0.5 favors precision, for problems with a genuine asymmetric cost.
F1 Score still ignores True Negatives entirely, since it is built purely from precision and recall, a gap Cohen Kappa addresses later.
It extends to multiclass problems via macro-averaging, weighted-averaging, or micro-averaging across per-class F1 scores.
Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score together offer complementary, genuinely different lenses on classifier quality.
